idiom_name: well-known symbols and runtime protocols (Symbol.iterator, Symbol.toPrimitive, Symbol.hasInstance)
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no types to select on, so the property that decides behaviour is the protocol an object implements: a function under a well-known symbol, or simply a method of the expected name. The language itself dispatches on these protocols - for...of calls obj[Symbol.iterator](), + and template literals call [Symbol.toPrimitive] (falling back to valueOf/toString), x instanceof C consults C[Symbol.hasInstance], Promise resolution adopts any thenable, and Array.isArray is a built-in brand check - so the replacement for a descriptor is to define the behaviour under the symbol-keyed method on each type and let generic code call the protocol instead of branching on the type. Where a property is a constant rather than an operation (codec name, element kind), it lives in a table keyed by the constructor, since the type at runtime is just the constructor function.
pitfalls: A protocol check is a shape check: any object with a callable then is treated as a thenable by await and Promise (and an object with a callable [Symbol.iterator] is iterable), so a typo in a property name turns into a behaviour switch rather than an error.

Well-known symbols are shared global state: patching Symbol.iterator or Symbol.hasInstance on a built-in prototype changes behaviour for every unrelated consumer of that prototype, and using a non-well-formed iterable throws a TypeError at the call site, not where the type was described.

instanceof walks the prototype chain and consults Symbol.hasInstance, so it fails across realms and with proxies; use Array.isArray, typeof, or an explicit brand check where a property test must be reliable.
